part.fundamentos.title: Angular Accessibility Fundamentals
part.fundamentos.summary: First part of the accessibility documentation for Angular applications, VoiceOver and TalkBack.
sec.fundamentos.o-que-e-acessibilidade.s: Accessibility is a digital product being usable by everyone, regardless of visual, hearing, motor, cognitive or temporary limitations.
sec.fundamentos.o-que-e-acessibilidade.0: Accessibility is the capacity of a digital product to be used by every person, regardless of visual, hearing, motor, cognitive or temporary limitations.
sec.fundamentos.o-que-e-acessibilidade.1: A person with low vision using zoom.
A person with reduced mobility using the keyboard.
A person with a cognitive disability.
A person with an injured arm using only one hand.
sec.fundamentos.wcag-2-2.title: WCAG 2.2
sec.fundamentos.wcag-2-2.summary: WCAG is the most widely used standard in the world for evaluating digital accessibility. AA is the level most companies target.
sec.fundamentos.wcag-2-2.0.text: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the most widely used set of guidelines in the world for evaluating digital accessibility.
sec.fundamentos.pour.title: POUR
sec.fundamentos.pour.summary: Every WCAG criterion comes from four pillars: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
sec.fundamentos.pour.0.text: Every WCAG criterion derives from four pillars:
sec.fundamentos.pour.2.item.0: The user has to be able to perceive the content.
sec.fundamentos.pour.2.item.2: Information cannot depend on colour alone.
sec.fundamentos.pour.4.item.0: The interface has to be usable.
sec.fundamentos.leitores-de-tela-2.title: Screen readers
sec.fundamentos.leitores-de-tela-2.summa: TalkBack on Android, VoiceOver on iOS. Both need three things to work: an accessible name, the right role, and the right state.
sec.fundamentos.leitores-de-tela-2.1.tex: The native screen reader on Android.
sec.fundamentos.leitores-de-tela-2.3.tex: The native screen reader on iOS.
sec.fundamentos.leitores-de-tela-2.4.tex: What do they need in order to work correctly?
sec.fundamentos.como-um-leitor-de-tela-e: How does a screen reader see a page?
Not the way sighted users do. They move through headings, buttons, links, fields and landmarks — a visually perfect screen can be unusable.
These users do not see the interface the way sighted users do.
A visually perfect screen can be completely unusable with a screen reader.
sec.fundamentos.regra-de-ouro-da-acessib: Semantic HTML first, ARIA second. If a native tag solves the problem, use it — you get role, keyboard and state for free.
Always prefer semantic HTML before reaching for ARIA.
If a native HTML tag can solve the problem, use it.
sec.fundamentos.estrutura-semantica-basi: header, nav, main and footer give a screen reader the map of the page before a single line is read.
sec.fundamentos.landmarks.title: Landmarks
sec.fundamentos.landmarks.summary: Landmarks let screen readers jump straight to the important regions of the page instead of reading through everything.
sec.fundamentos.landmarks.0.text: Landmarks let screen readers navigate quickly through the important regions of the page.
sec.fundamentos.headings.title: Headings
sec.fundamentos.headings.summary: Headings form a navigation tree. Skipping a level suggests a structure that does not exist and disorients the reader.
sec.fundamentos.accessible-name.title: Accessible Name
sec.fundamentos.accessible-name.summary: Every interactive element needs a name. It comes from visible text, or from aria-label when there is no text to use.
sec.fundamentos.accessible-name.0.text: Every interactive element must have an accessible name.
sec.fundamentos.accessible-description.s: aria-describedby adds a hint alongside the name. The screen reader reads the field name and then the description.
sec.fundamentos.accessible-description.1: The screen reader will combine the field name with its description.
sec.fundamentos.nome-role-estado.title: Name + Role + State
sec.fundamentos.nome-role-estado.summary: Almost every screen reader problem comes down to three questions: what is the name, what is the role, what is the state.
sec.fundamentos.nome-role-estado.0.text: Almost any screen reader analysis can be reduced to three questions:
sec.fundamentos.erros-mais-comuns-encont: The most common mistakes in Angular
Clickable divs, unlabelled icon buttons, placeholder-only inputs, missing headings, modals without focus management, and positive tabindex.
A clickable div pretending to be a button.
A clickable icon with no aria-label.
An input with only a placeholder.
A modal with no focus management.
Form errors that are never announced.
sec.fundamentos.mentalidade-para-o-time-: A mindset for the Angular team
Five questions to ask before building any component — they catch most accessibility problems before a single line is written.
Is there a native HTML tag for this?
Does the element have an accessible name?
Does it work with the keyboard?
